This verb is in turn derived from the prefix ana- (ἀνά), meaning 'up' or 'again,' and the verb stellō (στέλλω), meaning 'to stand' or 'to set.' In the context of Christian theology, anastellō is often used to describe the act of resurrection, particularly in reference to the resurrection of Jesus Christ. In the early Christian church, the name Anastellus was likely given to children born into families who saw the resurrection of Jesus as a central aspect of their faith. Today, the name Anastellus remains a powerful symbol of hope and redemption in the Christian tradition.

historical_references.reference: Anastasia of Sirmium was a Christian saint and martyr. She is traditionally believed to have been the daughter of Emperor Valentinian I and was born in Sirmium, now Sremska Mitrovica, Serbia. She is best known for surviving the persecution of Christians under Emperor Diocletian and for her refusal to marry the eldest son of the emperor, Valens, which led to her execution. Her feast day is celebrated on December 25.

Anastasia of Kiev was a Christian princess and a member of the Rurikid Dynasty of Kievan Rus'. She is believed to have been born in Kiev, Ukraine, and was the sister of Prince Svyatoslav I of Kiev. She is best known for her association with the famous icon of the Theotokos of Smolensk, which is said to have been discovered miraculously by her maidservant, and her role in spreading Christianity in Eastern Europe.
